title: Getting Started with bml
text: bml package estimates micro--macro regressions: Bayesian multilevel models aggregation member-level records group-level outcomes explicit, estimable object. Instead aggregating lower-level data higher levels assumed rule (risking aggregation bias) disaggregating outcomes lower levels (artificially inflating sample size), bml models lower-level units jointly shape higher-level outcomes — including members count (weights) contributions combine (aggregation function).

text: first model examines coalition duration function party-level characteristics, aggregated using equal weights: Breaking formula: Surv(dur_wkb, event_wkb): Survival outcome (duration event indicator) majority: Government-level covariate (binary indicator) id = id(pid, gid): Party ID (member) government ID (group) vars = vars(finance): Party-level attribute w = w(~ 1/n, scale = TRUE): weights — counts (equal weights, normalized sum 1) fn = fn("sum"): aggregation function — contributions combine (additive weighted mean; default) RE = TRUE: Party-specific random intercepts (shorthand RE = re(1)) feature’s coefficient appears output A_finance — ordinary class-"b" coefficient main model.

title: Getting Started with bml
text: Multiple-membership structure: Higher-level units (coalitions) contain multiple lower-level units (parties), lower-level units can appear multiple higher-level units. id(member, group) uses long format: one row per membership, number members per group. Weights w() — counts: within-group measure members. Fixed (w(~ 1/n)), observed (w(~ importance, scale = TRUE)), estimated (w(~ ilogit(b0 + b1 * q))). scale = TRUE normalizes weights sum 1 within group. Aggregation function fn() — contributions combine: fn("sum") additive case; fn("var"), fn("hhi"), fn("threshold"), fn("smax"), fn("gmean"), fn("cov") emergent features; fn(~ E(...)) user-written DSL. Parameters act external member characteristics belong w(); parameters act effect attribute belong fn(). Effects: member/unit random effects RE = re(1 + x) (partial pooling; cor = TRUE opts correlated intercept-slope), fixed effects FE = fe(1 + x) (pooling). hm() adds hierarchical nesting; unit-level covariates go main formula (Y ~ gdp + hm(id(cid), RE = re(1 + gdp))). Named blocks: give block name = reference feature interactions (Ax:education, Ax:Vx).

what: 1. What’s the difference between a multiple-membership model and a conventional multilevel model?
title: Frequently Asked Questions
text: conventional hierarchical multilevel model, lower-level unit belongs exactly one higher-level unit (e.g., students nested schools). multiple-membership model (MMMM), lower-level units can belong multiple higher-level units simultaneously, alternatively, higher-level outcomes can influenced multiple lower-level units. example: Conventional MLM: Students (level 1) nested schools (level 2) — student attends exactly one school. MMMM: Coalition governments (level 2) composed multiple political parties (level 1) — party can participate multiple governments time, government comprises multiple parties. MMMM accounts complex membership structure weighting contributions lower-level unit, allowing researchers model multiple units jointly shape higher-level outcomes.

Endogenize weight matrices: Rather imposing spatial network weights externally, let data determine connection strengths functions covariates. flexibility enables researchers explicitly model micro--macro link — lower-level characteristics aggregate produce higher-level outcomes.

Identification: internal parameters reach outcome b * feature; feature's coefficient ~0 unidentified. Lower values (e.g., 10) capture short-range dependence; higher values assess whether chain mixed well longer intervals. lag greater equal number stored draws per chain (e.g., n.thin > 1 reduced number stored draws), automatically lowered warning.

title: Summarize MCMC convergence diagnostics — mcmcDiag
text: Internally, function converts retained parameter draws coda::mcmc.list, computes per-chain diagnostics averages across chains parameter: Gelman–Rubin (\(\hat{R}\)): coda::gelman.diag().         Values close 1 indicate convergence; common heuristic         \(\hat{R} \le 1.1\). Geweke z-score: coda::geweke.diag().         Large absolute values (e.g., \(|z|>2\)) suggest lack convergence. Heidelberger–Welch p-value: coda::heidel.diag() tests         null stationarity chain segment. Autocorrelation: coda::autocorr() specified         lag, averaged across chains. Values near zero indicate good         mixing; persistent autocorrelation suggests chain needs thinning         reparameterization. statistics rounded three decimals. returned table transposed rows diagnostics columns parameters.

title: Random effects: partial pooling — re
text: Specifies random-effect structure mm hm block, mirroring left-hand side lme4/brms ( ... | group ) term. grouping implied block's id() therefore repeated. default cor = FALSE deliberately diverges brms's correlated default: correlated draw real JAGS cost, mm() blocks member random effects read weighted aggregate sum_k w_k u_k, correlation rarely interest often weakly identified. Opt cor = TRUE (supported single slope, .e. 2x2 case).
code: RE = TRUE            # shorthand for re(1) re(1)                # random intercept re(1 + x)            # intercept + slope on x (INDEPENDENT, the default) re(1 + x, cor = TRUE)# intercept + slope, correlated (lme4/brms `|`) - opt-in re(0 + x)            # slope only (also re(x - 1)) re(1, ar = TRUE)     # random walk over participation order re(1, ar = year)     # random walk over calendar time (gap-scaled variance)

title: Random effects: partial pooling — re
text: x effects expression: 1, 1 + var, 0 + var, var - 1. mm() blocks, slope variables member-level columns; hm() blocks main-level columns varying within nesting units. cor Logical; TRUE, intercept slope get joint bivariate-normal prior (correlated). Default FALSE (independent). ar Autoregressive random walk intercept across unit's repeated participations/observations. FALSE (default): independent effects. TRUE: random walk participation order, \(u_t \sim N(u_{t-1}, \sigma^2)\). unquoted column name (e.g. ar = year): random walk (numeric) time variable, step variance scaled normalized time gaps, \(u_t \sim N(u_{t-1}, \sigma^2 \, \Delta_t / \bar\Delta)\) — equal spacing reproduces ar = TRUE model, \(\sigma\) keeps per-average-step interpretation. Requires intercept-re(1); time values must unique within unit.

text: Variance decomposition. total variance outcome partitioned additive components, one level model: $$\mathrm{Var}(y) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \ldots$$ component contributes variance \(\sigma^2\), except multiple-membership (MM) levels, effective variance contribution scaled average summed squared weights across groups. $$\mathrm{Var}_{\mathrm{mm}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{mm}}^2 \cdot \overline{w^2}, \quad \overline{w^2} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{=1}^{N} \sum_{k} w_{ik}^2$$ weight adjustment accounts fact member-level variance distributed across multiple members potentially unequal influence. equal weights (\(w_{ik} = 1/n_i\)), effective variance shrinks group size increases. Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). ICC given level proportion total variance attributable level: $$\rho_l = \frac{\sigma_l^2}{\sum_{l'} \sigma_{l'}^2}$$ Intuitively, ICC answers: "fraction total variation outcome due differences units level?" ICC 0.30 country level, example, means 30% outcome variation can attributed -country differences. ICCs computed per posterior draw summarized, properly propagating uncertainty MCMC samples. Family-specific handling: Gaussian / Weibull: residual sigma model     used directly. Binomial: residual sigma. latent logistic     residual variance \(\pi^2/3 \approx 3.29\) used instead. Cox: residual variance. ICCs computed among     non-residual components .
